entity.name: Constantine the Great
entity.description: The emperor who made Christianity Rome's religion. Constantine won a civil war, legalized Christian worship with the Edict of Milan in 313, convened the Council of Nicaea, and founded Constantinople as a new capital that lasted over a thousand years. He was only baptized on his deathbed.

story.name: Constantine the Great
story.description: Proclaimed emperor by his troops in York, victorious at the Milvian Bridge, legalizer of Christianity at Milan, founder of Constantinople. The emperor who remade the Roman world.

moments.name: Constantine Is Born in the Roman Provincial City of Naissus
moments.subtitle: The son of a Roman officer and a Greek woman of low birth who would become a saint
moments.description: On February 27, 272 AD, Constantine was born in Naissus (modern Nis, Serbia), a city in the Roman province of Moesia Superior. His father Flavius Constantius was a Roman army officer who would rise to become one of the four emperors of the Tetrarchy. His mother Helena was a Greek woman of low social standing, possibly from Bithynia, whose legal status as wife or concubine remains uncertain. Helena would later be canonized as a saint. Constantine spent little time with his father, instead being sent to Emperor Diocletian's court as both heir presumptive and political hostage.

moments.name: Roman Troops Proclaim Constantine Emperor at York After His Father Dies
moments.subtitle: A son rushes across Europe to reach his dying father and inherits an empire
moments.description: In July 306 AD, Constantine's father Constantius died at Eboracum (modern York, England) after campaigning in Britain. Constantine, who had raced from Diocletian's court in the east to rejoin his father, was immediately proclaimed Augustus by his father's loyal troops. This act defied the Tetrarchic system of imperial succession established by Diocletian, which did not recognize hereditary claims. The proclamation launched nearly two decades of civil war among rival claimants. Constantine would not become sole ruler of the Roman Empire until 324 AD, but the moment at York set the trajectory of Western civilization.

moments.name: Constantine Issues the Edict of Milan Legalizing Christianity Across the Roman Empire
moments.subtitle: Three centuries of persecution end with a single imperial decree
moments.description: In February 313 AD, Constantine and his co-emperor Licinius met in Milan and proclaimed the Edict of Milan, which decriminalized Christian worship and ended the Great Persecution launched by Diocletian in 303. The edict granted religious tolerance throughout the empire, returning confiscated church property and establishing a precedent of imperial patronage of Christianity. Constantine had begun favoring Christianity after 312, though he would not be baptized until his deathbed in 337. The Edict of Milan marked the turning point in the Christianization of the Roman Empire and, ultimately, of Western civilization.

moments.name: Constantine Convenes 318 Bishops at the First Council of Nicaea
moments.subtitle: A Roman emperor who needed a Greek translator defines Christian theology for centuries
moments.description: In the summer of 325 AD, Constantine convened the First Council of Nicaea (modern Iznik, Turkey), gathering approximately 318 bishops to resolve theological disputes threatening Christian unity, particularly the Arian controversy over the nature of Christ. The council produced the Nicene Creed, a statement of belief that remains foundational to most Christian denominations nearly 1,700 years later. Constantine presided over the proceedings despite needing a Greek translator for his Latin speeches. The council established a model of church-state relations in which the emperor, though not yet baptized, shaped Christian doctrine.

moments.name: Constantine Refounds Byzantium as Constantinople, the New Roman Capital
moments.subtitle: A city built to replace Rome endures as a capital for over 1,100 years
moments.description: On May 11, 330 AD, Constantine formally dedicated Constantinople (modern Istanbul) as the new capital of the Roman Empire, built on the site of the ancient Greek city of Byzantium. Officially named "New Rome," the city took on Constantine's name and became the political, economic, and cultural center of the empire. Constantine filled it with Christian churches alongside pagan monuments, creating a hybrid capital for a transitioning civilization. Constantinople served as the capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire for over 1,100 years until its fall to the Ottoman Turks in 1453.

moments.name: Constantine Is Baptized on His Deathbed at Nicomedia
moments.subtitle: The first Christian emperor waits until his final days to receive the sacrament
moments.description: On May 22, 337 AD, Constantine died at Nicomedia (modern Izmit, Turkey) shortly after finally receiving Christian baptism from Eusebius of Nicomedia, an Arian bishop. Despite favoring Christianity for 25 years, issuing the Edict of Milan, convening the Council of Nicaea, and building the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, Constantine had remained a catechumen throughout his reign. Deathbed baptism was not uncommon in the era, as it was believed to wash away all sins. Constantine left the empire to his sons, replacing Diocletian's meritocratic Tetrarchy with dynastic succession.
